description: Doing the health challenge, so interested in health and coding!
summary:
On a Mars mission, Earth communication can take upwards of 20-30 minutes… unsuitable for a surgeon/medical specialist back home to communicate during emergencies.

WIASE, named after the Twi word Cosmos, is the crew's personal health console! It tracks each astronaut's physiological levels, evaluating them in combination with environmental data across the cabin. 

When a concerning change persists, WIASE’s algorithm alerts the team with visual reference to interactive 3D anatomy model of each astronaut's body, or the cabin map.  By analyzing environmental metrics like CO2, temperature/humidity, and human measurements like heart rate, blood pressure, SpO2, sleep, reaction time, against that astronaut's measured baseline. These baselines and simulated astronaut/environment bot data were calibrated from open datasets, including NASA ISS cabin data (EDA RR-6) and NASA RadLab radiation records.

However, it also educates the team on what exactly is wrong, and the steps they can take to fix it- acting in place of a medical expert ‘till Earth communication is received. It runs fully offline, simulates the communication delay, and includes a dashboard “to-do” mission checklist along with a 45-second reaction test and a daily wellbeing check-in that informs its health algorithms. 

WIASE keeps you safe far within the cosmos!
details:
How to use it?

First, you can hit the “tour” button on top-right to get an idea of interface/features. Then you’re free to explore on your own or “simulate” a real space mission scenario!

What does it do?

Using NASA ISS cabin (OSDR EDA) and radiation (RadLab) records (and external data), WIASE provides a dashboard for astronauts to understand environmental and physiological health conditions along with plan tasks, see data trends, and current conditions

How does it work?

  1. Four bots, (3 astronauts, 1 cabin) simulate real time data (which would be replaced by real astronaut / cabin sensors during mission) 
  2. Computes this data against baselines in the app’s internal alerting algorithm, and triggers a potential alert if concerning trend emerges
  3. It delays slightly to filter, as the  reading must stay out of range for a set time before it counts as an alert. The cognitive alert also needs 2 of 3 signals to agree, which cuts false alarms
  4. Shows physiological problems on the body and environmental ones on the cabin map, with the steps to take
  5. Additional features: Mission To-do list, cognitive tests / daily health check ins so the crew can track their own trends, displays past data/trends.

What benefits?

If crews had WIASE, they could…

  1. Work without earth communication for the delay until health experts consult back (which can take up to 22 minutes each way). When emergencies need timely response, it's great to have.
  2. Automatic trend detection: if something is wrong, crew is alerted, mitigating failure to see and address issues
  3. Customizable to individual: Algorithm compares individual baselines which will be collected in space, to have an accurate view of an individual's healthy, steady state in space
  4. Runs anywhere, it's a lightweight browser app that also works offline on relatively weak laptops (without installs, accounts, etc.)

Intended impact for project:

To help astronauts and space missions during the communication gap/delay. This can help them have a synced view of their environment (cabin) and internal state, informing them of potentially problematic trends and what to do about it. 

What tools are used?

  • Python 3: Runs the server, simulates crew and cabin data, and applies the alert rules. Uses only the standard library.
  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS: Power the dashboard directly in the browser using plain code, with no framework or build step.
  • three.js: Draws the 3D body and the crew thumbnails.
  • Blender: Turned the open Z-Anatomy model into the 3D body used in the app.
  • Python unittest and Node’s test runner: Run automated tests for the server and dashboard code.
  • Headless Chrome: Automatically clicked through the site to check features and layouts.
  • Claude Code: Helped write and test the code. The idea and design are the team’s.
  • Git and GitHub: Handle version control and code hosting.

How is the project creative?

  • Health on a real body: instead of charts, WIASE lights up the actual organs and nerves involved on a 3D anatomy model, like the brainstem and vagus nerve for heart rate or the bone marrow for radiation. You can see at a glance which part of someone is under strain.
  • Body and cabin together: each astronaut's readings sit next to the shared cabin air. When CO2 rises, everyone's lungs light up at once, so it's clear the problem is shared, and integration of both environment and physiology is relatively rare (from what we found).
  • See how an alert was detected: you can step through the moments an alert formed, from crossing the person's own limit to confirmation and recovery. The crew sees the reasoning, not just a warning, which matters when there's no doctor to call.
  • A reaction test that's a game: each trial randomly picks one of three mini-games, so it's harder to memorise and less of a chore to do every day, and it still measures reaction time properly.
  • Built for the delay: in Deep Space mode, messages from Earth arrive minutes late, so the app is designed for the crew to act first.
  • It teaches as it guides: every response explains why the problem is different in space. For example, exhaled CO2 can collect around your face because air doesn't rise without gravity. So the crew knows what to do in crisis (not just whats wrong)

Supplemental Materials:

  • We tried to contain design constraints to make an aesthetic dashboard while also being functional:
    • Cool graphics that inform (bird-eye view of cabin + perspective human anatomy)
    • Cohesive color scheme
    • Only important / high ROI functions rather than lots of features
    • Personalized to cabin and individuals
    • Informative: contains enough information to be useful during emergencies
    • Simulate real life: bots should mimic real-life expected data values & scenarios
    • Relevant info: several hours were spent researching most feasible data to collect that would give us most insight on the most pressing health problems NASA lists in space.
  • Inspiration:
    • We designed the dashboard for functionality, which also meant removing a lot of unnecessary information so the team knows all that they need to know, and extra information does not clog their mind. The line between too much and too little information was a constant consideration we kept in mind while creating our product
    • Design choice not to have a scrollable dashboard, so astronauts would not miss information/alerts. Similarly we split the dashboard into 5 sections, top bar, top left, top right, etc. to have predictable and separated information streams. 
    • We selected a specific color / design palette to make the website feel more coherent and overall less distracting + more enjoyable to work in
  • Future Improvements:
    • Adding a side-by-side comparison of an astronaut in its previous state (e.g. 1+ hours ago) and in its current state.
    • making the cognitive alert sensitive to smaller changes (right now it only catches the full change)
    • testing with real wearable data (also we never collected dashboard UI/UX feedback, and we would be biased as we developed so that data is useful too)
    • cross-crew patterns: if two people slow down while CO₂ is up, it points to the cabin
  • Extra:

Grand Source List

NASA Data

  • NASA OSDR Environmental Data App — ISS RR-6 cabin telemetry for CO₂, temperature, and humidity. Data app
  • NASA OSDR RadLab API — ISS DosTel1 radiation dose rate. Data API

Non-NASA Data

  • BIDSleep 1.0.1 (Song et al., 2026, PhysioNet) — Sleep stages and sleep heart rate. Dataset
  • Pulse Transit Time PPG Dataset 1.1.0 (Mehrgardt et al., 2022, PhysioNet) — Heart rate, SpO₂, and blood pressure. Dataset
  • QoL_Stress 1.0.0 (Calvo et al., 2026, PhysioNet) — STAI-S anxiety scores. Dataset
  • Resting-state EEG Dataset for Sleep Deprivation (Xiang et al., OpenNeuro ds004902) — Reaction-test times and lapses. Dataset
  • Smart Home Dataset (Zafar et al., figshare) — Included in the workbook only. Dataset
  • Wearable Device Dataset 1.0.1 (Hongn et al., 2025, PhysioNet) — Included in the workbook only. Dataset
